candidates.attacker_control: A remote service endpoint, or any server able to return an HTTP 3xx response to the CXF client, controls the Location header (and Set-Cookie headers on the 3xx response). The Location is parsed verbatim in extractLocation and converted to absolute form in convertToAbsoluteUrlIfNeeded before being used to create a new connection.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: autoRedirect is not enabled by the JAX-RS ClientImpl unless the http.autoredirect property is supplied, so the JAX-RS default may be off. The generated HTTPClientPolicy/schema is absent from this snapshot, so its exact default could not be confirmed. checkAllowedRedirectUri does provide same-host and allow-list protections, but only when explicitly configured; AUTO_REDIRECT_SAME_HOST_ONLY is read without a default (HTTPConduit.java 1816). removeAuthorizationHeaders mitigates ordinary Authorization headers, but preemptive credentials are deliberately re-added for the redirect target. Relative redirects are rejected unless http.redirect.relative.uri is enabled. I did not execute code or tests, and no runtime confirmation was possible.
candidates.impact: A malicious or compromised server can cause the CXF client to issue HTTP(S) requests to arbitrary internal/external hosts reachable from the client process (SSRF), leak preemptive Authorization credentials and maintained session cookies to the redirect target, and durably change the client base address so later requests are sent to the attacker-controlled host. This can expose internal services, credentials, session material, or allow unauthorized actions on the redirected service.
candidates.prerequisites: The client must follow redirects (HTTPClientPolicy.autoRedirect or the http.autoredirect property). The same-host guard is bypassed by default unless http.redirect.same.host.only=true or http.redirect.allowed.uri is configured. Credential exposure additionally requires a preemptive AuthorizationPolicy (Basic/Digest) or maintainSession with stored cookies. The redirected host must be reachable by the client process.
candidates.root_cause: HTTPConduit follows server-supplied redirect Location values to arbitrary schemes/hosts when autoRedirect is enabled. The same-host restriction in checkAllowedRedirectUri is only enforced when the caller sets http.redirect.same.host.only or an allowed-URI property; it is not the default. redirectRetransmit removes normal Authorization headers but then re-adds credentials from the configured preemptive AuthorizationPolicy for the attacker-selected URI, writes maintained-session cookies into the redirected request, records transport.retransmit.url, and AbstractClient later adopts that URL as the client base URI.
candidates.title: Cross-host HTTP redirect handling enables SSRF, credential/cookie leak, and persistent client rebasing
candidates.trace: 1) WrappedOutputStream.processRetransmit sees 301/302/303/307 and calls redirectRetransmit (HTTPConduit.java 1434-1445). 2) extractLocation returns the raw server Location (HTTPConduit.java 1000-1014), and convertToAbsoluteUrlIfNeeded accepts any value beginning with http (HTTPConduit.java 1844-1858). 3) checkAllowedRedirectUri only rejects a different scheme/host when the non-default http.redirect.same.host.only property is set; otherwise no host validation occurs (HTTPConduit.java 1816-1837). 4) The code removes Authorization headers, then setHeadersByAuthorizationPolicy re-adds credentials for the new URI (1476-1487, 790-806), calls cookies.writeToMessageHeaders (1488), records transport.retransmit.url and invokes retransmit(newURL) (1489-1490). 5) URLConnectionHTTPConduit.setupNewConnection constructs a new Address from newURL and opens an HttpURLConnection to it (414-429). 6) AbstractClient.completeExchange consumes transport.retransmit.url and rebases the client state/current builder to it (546-559), so subsequent JAX-RS calls can continue to target the attacker-selected host.
candidates.unverified: Whether the deployed/default HTTPClientPolicy enables autoRedirect; whether the target deployment sets same-host/allowed-URI restrictions; whether maintainSession/cookies or preemptive AuthorizationPolicy are configured; and whether all alternate conduits (async/netty) share the same redirect and cookie behavior. The candidate is a source-level lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.
candidates.weakness_type: Server-Side Request Forgery (CWE-918) with credential/cookie exposure

coverage_summary: Inspected the source-scope report (4,768 files; no binary/sensitive-name/oversize/symlink exclusions) and sampled all major module families: core XML/STAX/DOM and resource resolvers, HTTP/HTTPS transports, JAX-RS client and providers, JAX-WS/STS, OAuth1/OAuth2/OIDC/SAML/JOSE security modules, attachment/MIME parsing, WSDL tooling/validation, and distribution samples. Focused reads covered redirect state machines, TLS hostname verification, certificate constraints, OAuth callback/token redirects, SAML response validation, CORS, XSLT providers, and MIME boundary parsers. Tests and generated classes (including HTTPClientPolicy) are not in the visible snapshot, so generated defaults and runtime configurations could not be verified.
limitations: Source-only review; no code execution, tests, scanners, or runtime confirmation was performed.
Tests are absent from the snapshot and generated JAXB/schema classes (e.g., HTTPClientPolicy) are not visible, so default policy values and exact runtime behavior could not be confirmed.
No git metadata/build artifacts were available to map the snapshot to a specific upstream commit or CVE/fix.
Only bounded file ranges were read; not every one of the 4,768 files was inspected line-by-line, so additional unconfirmed issues may exist.

The single candidate is a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability; exploitability depends on client configuration such as autoRedirect, same-host/allowed-URI restrictions, maintainSession/cookies, and preemptive AuthorizationPolicy.

rejected_leads.lead: Reflected XSS through the service list page base URL / Host header in FormattedServiceListWriter (rt/transports/http/.../servicelist/FormattedServiceListWriter.java 121-127, 173-177, 194-195) and through WADL base URI output in WadlGenerator.java 256-291.
rejected_leads.reason: The code writes base paths/URLs into HTML/XML without escaping, but exploitability depends on container acceptance of malicious Host/path data, the service-list page being reachable, and browser rendering. It is a plausible lead but has weaker end-to-end attacker control than the redirect path.

rejected_leads.lead: OAuth 1.0 callback prefix check in RequestTokenHandler.validateCallbackURL (rt/rs/security/oauth-parent/oauth/src/main/java/org/apache/cxf/rs/security/oauth/services/RequestTokenHandler.java 124-148): oauthCallback.startsWith(client.getApplicationURI()) can accept https://trusted.example.evil.
rejected_leads.reason: The validation is explicitly intended to allow callbacks sharing a common root with the application URI, and exploitation requires a registered client with an empty callback URI and non-empty application URI. The verifier is later redirected in AuthorizationRequestHandler.java 150-156, but attacker prerequisites and exact registration semantics are uncertain.

rejected_leads.lead: STS/WS-MEX address handling in STSUtils.java 132-160 and AbstractSTSClient.configureViaEPR (491-519) can use an EPR-provided WSA address as the WS-Trust/MEX target, potentially sending credentials to an attacker-selected host.
rejected_leads.reason: A DISABLE_STS_CLIENT_WSMEX_CALL_USING_EPR_ADDRESS option is present (default false), and the EPR/policy usually comes from configuration or a WSDL whose trust level is deployment-specific. The attacker-control path is less direct than the HTTP redirect path.

rejected_leads.lead: MIME attachment parsing resource issues: unbounded header accumulation in AttachmentDeserializer.loadPartHeaders (324-378) and boundary/EOF index handling in MimeBodyPartInputStream.processBuffer (125-203).
rejected_leads.reason: Malformed multipart input may cause excessive memory use or boundary-related exceptions, but this is primarily a DoS lead and I did not establish a specific memory-exhaustion or crash path in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: XSLTJaxbProvider resolves the xslt.template contextual property via createTemplatesFromContext (rt/frontend/jaxrs/src/main/java/org/apache/cxf/jaxrs/provider/XSLTJaxbProvider.java 499-508), which could fetch remote stylesheets or read resources.
rejected_leads.reason: No source path shows a remote request parameter directly controlling that message-context property; exploitability depends on the embedding application populating it from untrusted input.

rejected_leads.lead: SAML SSO issuer prefix check in SAMLSSOResponseValidator.validateIssuer (169-179): issuerIDP.startsWith(issuer.getValue()) accepts short issuer prefixes.
rejected_leads.reason: Signature and trust-store validation still constrain assertion forgery, and the check may intentionally allow an entity ID that is a prefix of the configured SSO URL. No clear authentication bypass was demonstrated from source alone.

rejected_leads.lead: CORS filter reflects allow-listed/any Origin with Allow-Credentials when allowOrigins is empty (CrossOriginResourceSharingFilter.java 322-337, 390-417).
rejected_leads.reason: The empty-allowOrigins behavior appears intentional, and misuse requires a deployment choosing allowCredentials=true with no constrained origin list. No direct attacker-controlled bypass of configured origins was found.

rejected_leads.lead: X-Forwarded-For wrapper bug in AbstractHTTPServlet.java 481-485 (checks newRemoteAddr instead of originalRemoteAddr).
rejected_leads.reason: This causes the forwarded client address to be ignored (fail-closed) rather than trusted, so it does not create an exploitable spoofing condition.

summary: This is an Apache CXF 3.2.1-SNAPSHOT source snapshot (parent/pom.xml). Coverage filters left 4,768 model-visible files with no oversize, sensitive-name, symlink, or NUL-binary exclusions; tests and generated schema/JAXB classes (notably HTTPClientPolicy) are not present. I concentrated on HTTP transport redirect handling, JAX-RS client URI state, TLS hostname verification, attachment/MIME parsing, WSDL/URI resolution, OAuth/SAML/JOSE validation, and service/WADL output. The strongest source-backed candidate is HTTP client redirect handling: a remote server's 3xx Location can drive CXF to a different scheme/host, with optional-only same-host enforcement, re-attached preemptive credentials and session cookies, and persistent client rebasing. Other plausible leads were retained as rejected/unconfirmed because they are config-dependent, trust-dependent, or have weaker attacker-control traces.
